title: Developmental Trauma
subtitle: Threat during periods of rapid brain and relational development
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating developmental trauma across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain developmental trauma in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in developmental trauma.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to developmental trauma.

sections.explainSimply: Chronic adversity in childhood can affect learning, regulation, health and relationships.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Effects depend on timing, severity, caregiving, genetics, resources and later repair; outcomes are diverse rather than inevitable.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Research supports dose-related population risks, but “developmental trauma disorder” is not universally recognised as a formal diagnosis.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of developmental trauma as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need developmental trauma to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not use neuroscience to imply irreversible damage.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use developmental trauma to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses developmental trauma to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not use neuroscience to imply irreversible damage. Evidence classification: strong risk evidence; heterogeneous outcomes.
